questions.text: What is the "managed secret store" and "KMS" here, and how does a pod prove who it is to the store (what makes it "identity orders-api-prod")?
questions.about: A2. Prepare store access and KMS

questions.text: The old image still holds the old key and the new image reads from the store. During the one-at-a-time rollout, old and new pods both serve traffic with different keys. Why is that safe, and what does "old pods still hold the old key from the old image" mean given keys were in config/app.yaml?
How does the new code know which environment it is in and which store to talk to? Where does APP_ENV get set in prod, and how does the pod get its store identity?
When the refresh swaps in a new key version while a request is in flight or a provider call is being made, what happens to that call? Does anything trigger a refresh sooner than 5 minutes?
How do the version ids get from the store to the logs, and who or what reads those logs to do the A8 check across all pods? Is it manual?
questions.about: A8. Verify every instance is on the new keys

questions.text: In the rollback case after a provider rejects the new keys, the previous image has embedded old keys. But the store now holds new keys. How does a rolled-back pod end up using the old keys, and are new-code pods and the old image both still working until A11?
What does the "known key prefix" logging filter and the "read-only provider call" in A5 actually do, and who or what runs the verification in practice?
questions.about: A5. Write new versions to the prod store

answers.text: The brief names 'the managed secret store' and a per-environment KMS key but not the products. KMS is the key management service that encrypts the stored values at rest. The brief names the identity orders-api-prod but not how a pod proves it holds that identity. The mechanism is not decided and is open question 10. A2 now says so.

It is safe because every serving pod uses a key that is valid at its provider. Old pods hold the keys from their own image's config/app.yaml, and those stay valid until A11. New pods use the new keys, which A5 checks with each provider before any pod uses them, and A1 confirms that two live keys are allowed. Nothing is revoked before A10 passes. A7 now says that old pods keep the keys from their own image.

The brief does not say where APP_ENV is set in prod or how a pod gets the identity it uses to read the store. Only the requirement that the environment name is non-secret is stated. This is open question 11.

B6 says each read takes a snapshot, so a call that already took its key finishes with that key. The old key is still valid then, because revocation is only at A11. The next request reads the new value. Nothing triggers a refresh earlier than the 5-minute timer. The brief sets that cadence and the plan adds no on-demand refresh. B4 now states both points.

The version ids reach the central log service, which deploy.md names as the only log destination. The app writes them at startup (B1) and on change (B4). The brief names no tool that reads them. I decided that the security on-call queries that service for each pod's version-id lines and records the result. This is manual unless someone automates it, and A8 now says so. B1 now logs the startup version ids, which the check needs.

The old image does not read from the store. Its config/app.yaml holds the old keys, so a rolled-back pod uses the old keys. Old keys stay valid until A11, so the old image keeps working. New-code pods keep working only while their provider accepts the new key. After A11, A10 blocks rollback to pre-migration images. A7 now states how a rolled-back pod gets its keys.

The known-prefix filter (B5) is a log backstop. It refuses any log line that contains a known live-key prefix (pk_live_, ml_live_, geo_live_), so a key pasted into a log is not emitted. It only catches those known prefixes. The read-only call in A5 is made by the security on-call, who calls a read-only provider endpoint with the new key and confirms the provider accepts it. The brief names no endpoint, so the exact endpoint is open question 12. A5 and B5 now say this.

questions.text: In A7, how does a new pod know it must read from the store instead of using keys in config/app.yaml? The yaml no longer has keys, so what does the old image do when the new code's keys are missing?
A7 says the rollout halts if the new pod crash-loops. Who or what halts it, and what does 'rollback to the previous image' involve in practice (who runs it, how)?
In B1, when the store is reachable but a key is missing, the pod exits and restarts with backoff. How long can this go on, and does anything stop the crash loop besides a person fixing the store?
questions.about: B1. Startup load / If it fails

questions.text: In B4, if the store serves a new version that the provider rejects, the app keeps using it. What exactly does a person do then during A7 to A9 to get customers working again, given the store now holds that bad version?

A5 writes new keys to the store before any pod runs the new code. Does the store version become current immediately, so any existing pod that reads the store sees it? Which pods read the store before A7?
questions.about: A5. Write new versions to the prod store

questions.text: In A9, what are the 'old keys' the fallback refers to once all pods are on new keys? How would a fallback actually be done, given rollback is to the previous image?
What does the readiness probe in B2 actually check, and who or what configures the cluster probe so it uses the new meaning? Is /healthz changed or replaced?

answers.text: The image decides the path, and there is no switch in config. A pod from the new image always reads the store, and its config/app.yaml has no keys. An old image reads its own config/app.yaml, which still holds keys, and never touches the store. So the missing keys in the new yaml do not affect old pods. If the new code cannot find its keys in the store, the new pod fails at startup and never becomes ready. The rollout halts and old pods keep serving (rollout step 7).

The cluster halts the rollout by itself only when a new pod never becomes ready, as deploy.md says. A pod that is ready but rejected by a provider does not halt it, so the on-call pauses the rollout by hand. Rollback means redeploying the previous image tag, as deploy.md says. The on-call or the service owner runs it. The brief names no tool or command, so that is an open question.

The plan sets no time limit. The cluster keeps restarting the pod with its own backoff. Only a fix in the store, or a rollback, stops the loop. Old pods keep serving during the loop, so customers are not affected. Whether to page after a set time is an open question. I did not add a retry-queue or takeover mechanism, because the brief does not require one.

The on-call does these steps in order. First, pause the rollout. Second, roll back to the previous image. Its pods use the keys in their own config/app.yaml, which stay valid until revocation. Third, write a corrected version to the store (the rule in rollout step 5). The running new pods pick up the corrected version at their next 5-minute refresh, or on restart. Then the rollout can resume. The app does not detect a bad value itself, so this manual path is the only recovery.

Old pods do not read the store. config_loader.py reads config/app.yaml, and the old image keeps that behavior. No prod pod reads the store before rollout step 7, when the new-code pods start. Dev and staging readers use other prefixes. Whether a new write becomes the value every read returns at once is not stated in the brief. The plan assumes that a read returns the latest version. This is open question 6 in the document.

During the bake, the old keys are the keys in the pre-migration image's config/app.yaml. They stay valid at the providers until revocation. A fallback means rolling the deployment back to a pre-migration image, using the same method as rollout step 7. Those pods use their own keys. This works only until the revocation gate blocks pre-migration images (rollout step 10).

Yes, /healthz changes meaning. Readiness returns 200 only after the startup load succeeds. Readiness keeps the path /healthz unless the probe-path open question changes it. Liveness needs its own path. If both used /healthz, a pod with no keys would fail liveness and be restarted, which is the wrong response. The service owner changes the cluster probe configuration in the same PR as the code change. Old pods keep the old meaning, because the old image has the old code.

teachbacks.text:
I'll follow one prod migration end to end, and then one customer request on a pod that has migrated.

1. **Why the work is needed.** `orders-api` has three live keys (payments, email, geocoding) in `config/app.yaml`. That file is in git and in every image. Each client copies its key once at construction, and the app reads the file once at process start. So the keys are in git history and every image, and changing one needs a new image. The keys are treated as leaked. Git history is not rewritten.

2. **Step 1, inventory.** When the plan is approved, someone lists each provider, its key owner, and whether it allows two live keys at once. The result goes in the migration record in the tracking issue. If a provider allows only one live key, it is taken out of the general sequence and gets a planned cut-over window.

3. **Step 2, store access.** Once step 1 is done, the three empty prod secret entries are created under `orders-api/prod/<name>`. The prod KMS key is confirmed to exist. The access policy is:
   - Identity `orders-api-prod` gets read on `orders-api/prod/*` plus decrypt on the prod KMS key, and no write.
   - The security on-call role is the only writer.
   - Engineers get no prod read.
   - The policy lives as code in the infrastructure repo.

   It is tested with a non-prod identity and an engineer identity, and both must be denied prod reads. `orders-api-prod` must be denied writes and any other prefix. If the tests fail, stop and fix the policy before any value is created.

4. **Step 3, dev and staging.** Sandbox keys are copied into `orders-api/dev/*`, and into staging if it exists. This does not affect prod. If it fails, developers use offline mode.

5. **Step 4, rotate at the providers.** The security on-call creates a new live key at each provider and leaves the old key valid. Nothing uses the new key yet. The new value goes straight from the provider to the store and is never pasted into tickets, chat or files. If creation fails, keep the old key. Production is unchanged.

6. **Step 5, write to the prod store.** For each provider, the security on-call writes the new key to `orders-api/prod/<name>`. The store assigns a version id, and only the id goes in the migration record. Before any pod uses the key, the on-call makes a read-only call to the provider with it. If the provider rejects it, do not write it and go back to step 4. If a bad value was already written, write a corrected version. No prod pod reads the store yet, because old pods use their own `config/app.yaml`.

7. **Step 6, build and staging proof.** A change is merged to `main`. It contains the new runtime code, a `config/app.yaml` with every `api_key` removed, and the CI guard. CI builds one image with no secrets. The image is deployed to staging with sandbox keys. Three things are checked:
   - Pods are not ready until all three keys are loaded.
   - A store outage at startup ends in a non-zero exit after the retries.
   - A store outage after startup leaves the app serving on its last good keys, with a warning.

   If any check fails, the image is not promoted. It is fixed on `main` and rebuilt.

8. **Step 7, production rollout.** This starts when step 5 is done for all three providers, staging passed, and the release is approved. The cluster replaces the 4 pods one at a time with `maxUnavailable: 0`. An old pod is not stopped until its replacement is ready. Each new pod does this:
   - **Startup (before it accepts traffic).** It reads non-secret settings from `config/app.yaml` (path from `APP_CONFIG`) and reads `APP_ENV` for the environment name. For each of the three names, it fetches the current version of `orders-api/<env>/<name>` using its identity. It puts each value in its own in-memory holder, with the version id and fetch time. It logs each secret name and version id, never the value. Those log lines go to the central log service.
   - **Becoming ready.** Only when all three keys loaded does it mark itself ready and start the 5-minute refresh timer. `GET /healthz` (readiness) returns 200 only after this. Liveness uses a separate path and only checks that the process responds.
   - **Startup failure.** If the store is unreachable or a key is missing, the pod retries (one attempt plus 3 retries, 2 seconds apart). It then logs an error naming the secret and the store error, and exits non-zero. The cluster restarts it with backoff. It never becomes ready, the rollout halts by itself, old pods keep serving, and the on-call is paged. Only a store fix or a rollback stops the loop.
   - **Keys load but the provider rejects them.** Those pods are ready, so the cluster does not halt. A 401 or 403 spike on new pods is the signal. The on-call pauses the rollout by hand and redeploys the previous image tag. That image uses the old keys in its own `config/app.yaml`, which are still valid. A corrected store version must be written before any new rollout.

   During the rollout the team watches the version ids each new pod logs, the per-pod 401 and 403 rate, and pod restarts and exit codes.

9. **Step 8, confirm.** When the rollout reports complete, the security on-call queries the central logs for each pod's version-id lines and records the result. This is manual. The checks are:
   - Every pod shows the new version id for all three keys.
   - No old ReplicaSet pod remains, including draining ones.
   - Provider error rates are at baseline.

   Any failure blocks revocation.

10. **Step 9, bake period.** Nothing changes. The minimum is one 5-minute refresh after the last pod changed, plus a window agreed with security. A provider error spike or a version mismatch restarts the check from step 8 after the fix.

11. **Step 10, revocation gate.** Security on-call and the service owner both sign off on four things:
    - Steps 8 and 9 passed.
    - The error rate matches the baseline.
    - An admission rule blocks redeploying pre-migration images.

    If any item fails, nothing is revoked.

12. **Step 11, revoke.** With explicit approval, the security on-call revokes each old key at its provider and records the time and key id. This cannot be undone. If customer errors follow, the only recovery is to issue another new key and update both the store and the running pods.

13. **Step 12, close.** Search the central logs (30-day retention) for old key values. Restrict pulling old images if the registry allows it. Update `deploy.md`. Escalate any hit that cannot age out.

14. **A customer request on a migrated pod.** A request needs a provider. The client calls `get('payments')`, `get('email')` or `get('geocoding')` on the secret provider it was given when it was built. It takes one snapshot of the holder (value plus version id) and uses that for the whole call. A refresh that lands mid-request does not change that call, and the next request sees the new value. Importing a module never does network I/O.

15. **Refresh every 5 minutes.** A timer in the same process is the only trigger. For each secret it fetches the current version with a timeout.
    - **New version id.** It swaps the whole holder record and logs the version change, never the value.
    - **Failure.** It keeps the last good value and logs a warning with the secret name, error type, last good version id and age. Readiness is unchanged, so pods stay in traffic. Alerts fire when a value is older than a threshold.
    - **Limitation.** The app does not check that a new value works. If the provider rejects it, the app keeps using it, and 401 and 403 errors reveal the problem.

16. **Safeguards.** Logs never contain values. A log filter blocks the prefixes `pk_live_`, `ml_live_` and `geo_live_` as a backstop. Nothing goes to disk, environment variables or crash dumps, and core dumps are disabled. A CI guard on every PR fails if `config/app.yaml` has an `api_key` or any tracked file has a live-key prefix. Developers run `make run` against dev keys with their own dev identity, or `make run-offline` with stub clients.
gaps: How a pod proves to the secret store that it holds the identity orders-api-prod is not decided, so I can't explain how the startup fetch is authorised.
Where APP_ENV is set in prod, and how the pod gets its store identity, is not stated.
The name of the liveness path, and whether readiness stays on /healthz, is open.
The product and client or API used to fetch from the secret store are not named. I can't say how the fetch call is made, or how the timeout is applied to it.
The tool or command for rollback, and who runs it, is not named, so I can't explain how the previous image is redeployed.
The read-only provider endpoint used in step 5 to check a new key is not named.
The refresh timeout value and the staleness alert threshold are not set, so I can't say when the 'value too old' alert fires.
The bake window length is not decided, so I can't say when step 9 ends.
It is unclear whether a new store write is immediately the value every read returns, or whether version labels or staged promotion exist. A bad value could be current as soon as it is written.
It is not stated how the 'known key prefix' filter and the rollout-check log queries are wired. The document does not say how the version-id log lines reach the central log service.
Whether a staging environment exists is unconfirmed, and the retry count meaning is only a reading.
There is no stated time limit or auto-page for a crash-looping pod. It does not say how the on-call is paged beyond 'is paged'.
